OK I'm sure there are a lot of sites out ther that can explain this pretty well, but I'm just gonna shoot from the hip on this one.

DDoS means "Distributed Denial of Service". There are other kinds of denial of service attacks, but the goal of these types of attacks is to deny service. On the internet, denial of service means that people can't access the website that they are trying to get to. This can be done either by sending complete nonsense to the website's server to where it doesn't know how to respond, or just sending so many requests for web pages that the server can't keep up. In either case, the requests aren't from real users trying to use the site but from meanies who want to break the website.

The distributed part means that the attack is coming from a LOT of different computers. A very basic Denial of Service attack would be to just send a bunch of garbage data to a website until it stopped working. Since this has happened so many times in the past, people have learned how to prevent it from breaking their websites, so just sending crap data from one computer doesn't really do much anymore. However, a Distributed Denial of Service attack means that hundreds or maybe even thousands of computers are sending a bunch of garbage data to the website, making it sift through everything until it finds a real website request. Depending on how many computers are involved in the attack, this can take a very long time.

So in short, a DDoS attack is somebody using a bunch of computers to flood a website with fake page requests until it stops working.

DDoS stands for "distributed denial-of-service" and is a type of computer attach which overloads a target system.

Your computer communicates with a server to show you a website. Computer ---BEEP---> Server. The server communicates back. Server ---BOOP---> Computer. This is a major simplification but will work. So when you're browsing a site you get something like BEEP BOOP BEEP BEEP BOOP BEEP BOOP .. BEEP. The bigger the website, the more computers trying to send in their BEEPs and the server (or servers) have to try to keep up with sending out their BOOPs.

In a DoS (denial-of-service) attack, you make a computer send as many BEEPs as possible, simulating many computers trying to connect at once. This makes it very difficult for the server to respond with BOOPs. It'd be something like

BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BOOP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BOOP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP BEEP

I believe most large ISPs have bot detection and remediation protocols. There may be a lack of implementation that plays a role. But the main reason DDoSs are hard to thwart is because of the distributed nature - you've got tens, sometimes hundreds, of thousands of computers across the world all on different ISPs, all making legitimate requests, just really quickly. If an ISP blocks a few computers it doesn't have a vast impact. It makes sense to me that someone controlling a botnet would also try to avoid using 100% against a target, so that as computers are blocked they can just spool up more from reserves. I don't know much about the software that controls a bot or the scripts a bot would execute, but between the two there's likely some techniques used to make it seem as much like a legitimate computer as possible.
